L328: ## 4  Convergence Analysis
L329: 
L330: In this section, we establish a non-asymptotic convergence rate analysis for Doob’s matching (cite154†3.21 ) and the induced controllable diffusion model (cite159†3.23 ) introduced in Section cite14†3 .
L331: 
L332: ### 4.1  Assumptions
L333: 
L334: We begin by outlining the essential technical assumptions required for our theoretical results.
L335: ###### Assumption 1 (Bounded support).
L336: 
L337: The support of the target distribution $q_{0}$ is a compact set contained within the hypercube $\{\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}:\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty}\leq 1\}$.
L338: Assumption cite158†1 is a standard condition imposed on the data distribution (cite156†Lee et al., 2023a ; cite100†Oko et al., 2023 ; cite162†Chang et al., 2025a ; cite163†Beyler and Bach, 2025 ). This constraint is well-motivated by practical applications; for instance, image and video data consist of bounded pixel values, thereby satisfying this requirement.
L339: ###### Assumption 2 (Bounded weight function).
L340: 
L341: The weight function $w$ defined in (cite131†3.1 ) is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Specifically, there exist constants $0<\underline{B}<1<\overline{B}<\infty$ such that
L342: 
L343:  | $$\underline{B}\leq w(\mathbf{x})\leq\bar{B},\quad\text{for all}\penalty\ \mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{supp}(q_{0}).$$  |
L344: Assumption cite164†2 implies that the base distribution $p_{0}$ and the tilted distribution $q_{0}$ satisfy mutual absolute continuity, ensuring that their supports coincide (i.e., $\mathrm{supp}(p_{0})=\mathrm{supp}(q_{0})$). This condition is crucial for establishing the regularity of Doob’s $h$-function.
L345: Furthermore, the ratio $\kappa\coloneq\bar{B}/\underline{B}$ serves as a condition number that characterizes the difficulty of the controllable diffusion task, as discussed in the context of posterior sampling by cite60†Purohit et al. (2025) ; cite56†Ding et al. (2024b) ; cite52†Chang et al. (2025b) .
L346: ###### Assumption 3 (Base score estimation error).
L347: 
L348: The base score estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{s}}$ defined in (cite107†2.5 ) satisfies the following error bound:
L349: 
L350:  | $$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}h{\mathbb{E}}^{{\mathbb{P}}}\left[\|\widehat{\mathbf{s}}(kh,\mathbf{X}_{kh}^{\leftarrow})-\nabla\log p_{T-kh}(\mathbf{X}_{kh}^{\leftarrow})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{base}}^{2}.$$  |
L351: Assumption cite165†3 requires the $L^{2}$-error of the base score estimator $\widehat{\mathbf{s}}$ to be bounded with respect to the base path measure ${\mathbb{P}}$. In our setting, where numerous samples from the base distribution $p_{0}$ are available, estimators satisfying this bound can be obtained via implicit score matching (cite96†Hyvärinen, 2005 ), sliced score matching (cite97†Song et al., 2020 ), or denoising score matching (cite98†Vincent, 2011 ).
L352: While one can derive explicit bounds of base score matching as cite99†Tang and Yang (2024) ; cite100†Oko et al. (2023) ; cite101†Fu et al. (2024) ; cite102†Ding et al. (2024a) ; cite166†Yakovlev and Puchkin (2025a) ; cite167†Yakovlev et al.
L353: (2025) using non-parametric regression theory for deep neural networks (cite103†Bauer and Kohler, 2019 ; cite104†Schmidt-Hieber, 2020 ; cite105†Kohler and Langer, 2021 ; cite106†Jiao et al., 2023 ), we adopt this condition to maintain clarity of presentation, following the convention of cite156†Lee et al. (2023a) ; cite157†Chen et al. (2023) ; cite163†Beyler and Bach (2025) ; cite168†Kremling et al. (2025) .
L354: ### 4.2  Regularity of Doob’s $h$-function
L355: 
L356: In this subsection, we establish the regularity properties of Doob’s $h$-function defined in (cite141†3.10 ).
L357: ###### Proposition 4.1.
L358: 
L359: Suppose Assumptions cite158†1 and cite164†2 hold. Then for all $t\in(0,T)$ and $\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}$, the following bounds hold:
L360: 
L361:   1. (i)
L362: 
L363: $\underline{B}\leq h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\leq\bar{B}$;
L364: 
L365:   2. (ii)
L366: 
L367: $\max_{1\leq k\leq d}|D_{k}h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})|\leq 2\sigma_{T-t}^{-2}\bar{B}$; and
L368: 
L369:   3. (iii)
L370: 
L371: $\max_{1\leq k,\ell\leq d}|D_{k\ell}^{2}h_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})|\leq 6\sigma_{T-t}^{-4}\bar{B}$,
L372: where $D_{k}$ and $D_{k\ell}^{2}$ denote the first-order and second-order partial derivatives with respect to the input coordinates, respectively.
L373: The proof of Proposition cite169†4.1 is deferred to Appendix cite35†C.1 . It is worth noting that Proposition cite169†4.1 relies solely on the boundedness of the weight function $w$, without requiring the existence or smoothness of its gradients. Nevertheless, we establish that Doob’s $h$-function admits bounded derivatives.
L374: This result stems from the definition of Doob’s $h$-function as a posterior expectation under a Gaussian likelihood; the inherent smoothness of the Gaussian kernel endows the posterior expectation with strong regularity properties.
L375: ### 4.3  Error bounds for the Doob’s guidance estimator
L376: 
L377: We begin by introducing the concept of Rademacher complexity (cite170†Bartlett and Mendelson, 2002 ; cite171†Mohri et al., 2018 ), which is crucial for analyzing the generalization error.
L378: ###### Definition 1 (Rademacher complexity).
L379: 
L380: Let ${\mathscr{H}}$ be a function class, and let $\mathbf{X}^{1:n}\coloneq(\mathbf{X}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{X}^{n})$ be a set of samples. The empirical Rademacher complexity of ${\mathscr{H}}$ with respect to $\mathbf{X}_{1:n}$ is defined as
L381: 
L382:  | $$\widehat{{\mathfrak{R}}}({\mathscr{H}}|\mathbf{X}^{1:n})\coloneq{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sup_{h\in{\mathscr{H}}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon_{i}h(\mathbf{X}^{i})\Big|\mathbf{X}^{1:n}\Big],$$  |
L383: where $\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{n}$ are i.i.d. Rademacher random variables. The Rademacher complexity of ${\mathscr{H}}$ is the expectation of empirical Rademacher complexity with respect to the distribution of $\mathbf{X}^{1:n}$ defined as
L384: 
L385:  | $${\mathfrak{R}}_{n}({\mathscr{H}})\coloneq{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat{{\mathfrak{R}}}({\mathscr{H}}|\mathbf{X}^{1:n})]={\mathbb{E}}\Big[\sup_{h\in{\mathscr{H}}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon_{i}h(\mathbf{X}^{i})\Big].$$  |
L386: For notational simplicity, we define the derivative classes and their associated Rademacher complexity as follows:
L387: 
L388:  | $${\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\nabla{\mathscr{H}}_{t})\coloneq\sum_{k=1}^{d}{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(D_{k}{\mathscr{H}}_{t}),\quad D_{k}{\mathscr{H}}_{t}\coloneq\big\{D_{k}h_{t}:h_{t}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{t}\big\}.$$  |  | (4.1)
L389: 
L390: The following lemma provides an oracle inequality for the Doob’s matching.
L391: ###### Lemma 4.2 (Oracle inequality).
L392: 
L393: Suppose Assumptions cite158†1 and cite164†2 hold. Let $t\in(0,T)$ and let ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ be a convex hypothesis class. Let $\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}$ be the gradient penalized empirical risk minimizer defined as (cite154†3.21 ), and let $h_{t}^{*}$ be the Doob’s $h$-function defined as (cite141†3.10 ). Then the following inequalities hold:
L394:  |  | $\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\|\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}-h_{t}^{*}\|_{L^{2}(p_{T-t})}^{2}\Big]$  |
L395:  |  | $\displaystyle\lesssim\underbrace{\inf_{h_{t}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{t}}\|h_{t}-h_{t}^{*}\|_{H^{1}(p_{T-t})}^{2}}_{\text{approximation}}+\underbrace{\bar{B}{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}({\mathscr{H}}_{t})+\frac{\lambda\bar{B}}{\sigma_{T-t}^{2}}{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\nabla{\mathscr{H}}_{t})}_{\text{generalization}}+\underbrace{\frac{\lambda^{2}d^{2}\bar{B}^{2}}{\sigma_{T-t}^{8}}}_{\text{regularization}},$  |
L396:  |  | $\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\Big[\|\nabla\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}-\nabla h_{t}^{*}\|_{L^{2}(p_{T-t})}^{2}\Big]$  |
L397:  |  | $\displaystyle\lesssim\underbrace{\frac{1}{\lambda}\inf_{h_{t}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{t}}\|h_{t}-h_{t}^{*}\|_{H^{1}(p_{T-t})}^{2}}_{\text{approximation}}+\underbrace{\frac{\bar{B}}{\lambda}{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}({\mathscr{H}}_{t})+\frac{\bar{B}}{\sigma_{T-t}^{2}}{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\nabla{\mathscr{H}}_{t})}_{\text{generalization}}+\underbrace{\frac{\lambda d^{2}\bar{B}^{2}}{\sigma_{T-t}^{8}}}_{\text{regularization}},$  |
L398: where the notation $\lesssim$ hides absolute constants.
L399: 
L400: The proof of Lemma cite172†4.2 is deferred to Appendix cite36†C.2 . Both oracle inequalities for Doob’s $h$-function and its gradient decompose the error into three components: approximation error, generalization error, and regularization error.
L401: 
L402:   1. (i)
L403: The approximation error is defined as the minimal $H^{1}$-distance between functions in the hypothesis class ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ and the target function $h_{t}^{*}$, measuring the approximation capability of ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$.
L404: 
L405:   2. (ii)
L406: 
L407: The generalization error captures the error arising from finite-sample approximation, which vanishes as the number of samples approaches infinity.
L408: 
L409:   3. (iii)
L410: The regularization error is introduced by the gradient penalty in the objective functional, which causes the minimizer of the population risk to deviate from the exact Doob’s $h$-function $h_{t}^{*}$ (cite141†3.10 ).
L411: #### Comparison with oracle inequality of vanilla regression
L412: 
L413: Lemma cite172†4.2 is analogous to the oracle inequality found in regression problems. Let $\widehat{h}_{t}$ be the estimator of the Doob’s $h$-function obtained via vanilla regression (cite145†3.18 ). Informally, the following oracle inequality holds:
L414:  | $${\mathbb{E}}\Big[\|\widehat{h}_{t}-h_{t}^{*}\|_{L^{2}(p_{T-t})}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\underbrace{\inf_{h_{t}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{t}}\|h_{t}-h_{t}^{*}\|_{L^{2}(p_{T-t})}^{2}}_{\text{approximation}}+\underbrace{\bar{B}{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}({\mathscr{H}}_{t})}_{\text{generalization}}.$$  |  | (4.2)
L415: 
L416: Comparing (cite173†4.2 ) with Lemma cite172†4.2 reveals several crucial differences:
L417: 
L418:   1. (i)
L419: The approximation error in Lemma cite172†4.2 is measured in the $H^{1}$-norm, whereas in (cite173†4.2 ), it is measured in the $L^{2}$-norm. This distinction is natural because we require the estimator to converge in the $H^{1}$-norm; thus, simultaneous approximation of the function and its derivatives is essential.
L420: Simultaneous approximation using neural networks has been investigated in various contexts (cite174†Li et al., 2019 ; cite175†Gühring et al., 2020 ; cite176†Gühring and Raslan, 2021 ; cite177†Duan et al., 2022a ; cite178†Duan et al., 2022b ; cite179†Lu et al., 2022b ; cite180†Shen et al., 2022 ; cite181†Shen et al., 2024 ; cite182†Belomestny et al., 2023 ; cite183†Yakovlev and Puchkin, 2025b ).
L421:   2. (ii)
L422: In vanilla regression, the generalization error in (cite173†4.2 ) depends only on the complexity of the hypothesis class. In contrast, the generalization error bounds in Lemma cite172†4.2 also depend on the complexity of the derivative classes (cite184†4.1 ). This occurs because the objective functional of the gradient penalized Doob’s matching (cite153†3.19 ) includes the gradient norm term.

L425: The most significant difference lies in the regularization error. L426: This highlights the key advantage of our gradient penalized method: the gradient penalty is essential for guaranteeing simultaneous convergence of both the estimator value and its gradient. Additionally, there exists a trade-off with respect to $\lambda$ in the oracle inequality for $\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}$: a larger $\lambda$ leads to larger regularization error, while reduces the approximation and generalization errors.
L427: Given the oracle inequality for a general hypothesis class ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$, we consider the specifical case that ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ is chosen as a neural network class, with the aim of deriving non-asymptotic convergence rates. We begin by formally defining the neural network class.
L428: ###### Definition 2 (Neural network class).
L429: 
L430: A function implemented by a neural network $h:{\mathbb{R}}^{N_{0}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{N_{L+1}}$ is defined by
L431: 
L432:  | $$h(\mathbf{x})=T_{L}(\varrho(T_{L-1}(\cdots\varrho(T_{0}(\mathbf{x}))\cdots))),$$  |
L433: where the activation function $\varrho$ is applied component-wise and $T_{\ell}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathbf{A}_{\ell}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_{\ell}$ is an affine transformation with $\mathbf{A}_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N_{\ell+1}\times N_{\ell}}$ and $\mathbf{b}_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N_{\ell}}$ for $\ell=0,\ldots,L$. In this paper, we consider the case where $N_{0}=d+1$ and $N_{L+1}=1$. The number $L$ is called the depth of neural networks.
L434: Additionally, $S:=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}(\|\mathbf{A}_{\ell}\|_{0}+\|\mathbf{b}_{\ell}\|_{0})$ represents the total number of non-zero weights within the neural network. We denote by $N(L,S)$ the set of neural networks with depth at most $L$ and the number of non-zero weights at most $S$.
L435: The following theorem establishes the convergence rate of the estimated Doob’s guidance given in (cite155†3.22 ).
L436: ###### Theorem 4.3 (Convergence rate of Doob’s guidance).

L438: Suppose Assumptions cite158†1 and cite164†2 hold. Let $t\in(0,T)$. Set the hypothesis class ${\mathscr{H}}_{t}$ as

L440: &\max_{1\leq k\leq d}\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|D_{k}h_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq 2\sigma_{T-t}^{-2}\bar{B},\end{aligned}\right\}.$$  |  | (4.3)
L441: where $L={\mathcal{O}}(\log n)$ and $S={\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{d}{d+4}})$. Let $\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}$ be the gradient penalized empirical risk minimizer defined as (cite154†3.21 ), and let $h_{t}^{*}$ be the Doob’s $h$-function defined as (cite141†3.10 ). Then the following inequalities hold:
L442: 
L443:  | $${\mathbb{E}}\Big[\|\nabla\log\widehat{h}_{t}^{\lambda}-\nabla\log h_{t}^{*}\|_{L^{2}(p_{T-t})}^{2}\Big]\leq C\sigma_{T-t}^{-8}n^{-\frac{1}{d+4}},$$  |

L445: The proof of Theorem cite91†4.3 is deferred to Appendix cite38†C.4 . This theorem demonstrates that the $L^{2}$-error of the Doob’s guidance estimator (cite155†3.22 ) converges to the exact Doob’s guidance in (cite139†3.14 ) as the sample size increases, provided that the size of the neural network is appropriately chosen.
L446: However, since the prefactor $\sigma_{T-t}^{-8}$ diverges as $t$ approaches the terminal time $T$, early stopping in controllable diffusion models (cite159†3.23 ) is required to ensure the validity of the Doob’s guidance estimator.
L447: ### 4.4  Error bounds for the controllable diffusion models
L448: 
L449: In this subsection, we establish a non-asymptotic convergence rate for the controllable diffusion models (cite159†3.23 ). We begin by presenting an error decomposition for the KL-divergence between the early-stopping distribution $q_{T_{0}}$ and the distribution of $\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{T-T_{0}}^{\leftarrow}$.
L450: ###### Lemma 4.4 (Error decomposition).
